slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 25: Appendix D — A Bounded, Transactional Reporting Application. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Appendix D — A Bounded, Transactional Reporting Application changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: D.1 Define the extension’s contract
keyPoints: The compact Chapter 21 application is the starting point.

The following contract applies to harbor_reports, not retroactively to every earlier example.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 25, treat D.1 Define the extension’s contract as a design decision with costs and evidence. The compact Chapter 21 application is the starting point. This extension retains its task-reporting purpose while making input limits, structured failures, and publication boundaries more explicit. Its implementation is separate so the reader can compare two designs without losing the simpler reference. The following contract applies to harbor_reports, not retroactively to every earlier example. An input record contains id|priority|done|title. The ID is a positive representable int, unique within the candidate dataset. Priority is one through three. Completion is zero or one. Numeric fields require whole-field conversion: a leading plus sign, surrounding whitespace, or trailing characters is rejected by this grammar. Leading zeros are accepted. Negative numeric syntax may parse, but negative values fail the relevant domain checks. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: D.2 Inspect the public boundary
keyPoints: Task is a simple transfer value; its fields are public so snapshots are easy to inspect.
The invariant belongs to the private accepted collection inside Report, which only receives validated tasks.
Constructing an arbitrary Task in a caller does not insert it into that collection.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 25, treat D.2 Inspect the public boundary as a design decision with costs and evidence. Task is a simple transfer value; its fields are public so snapshots are easy to inspect. The invariant belongs to the private accepted collection inside Report, which only receives validated tasks through load. Constructing an arbitrary Task in a caller does not insert it into that collection. This is a deliberate boundary: the application does not claim that every possible standalone task object is valid at every moment. The API returns copied snapshots and completed text. It does not expose mutable accepted storage or iterators that survive replacement. Error objects own only a code and line number, while diagnostic strings come from fixed literals. These choices keep ownership understandable at the cost of some copying, which is appropriate for the bounded instructional workload. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: D.3 Follow parsing, validation, and commit
keyPoints: The bounded reader retains at most the configured number of characters in its line string.
It reads one additional non-newline character to detect an overlong record but does not append it.
The input is not drained after rejection.
This gives a concrete retained-line bound without promising a precise process-memory ceiling: string capacity.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 25, treat D.3 Follow parsing, validation, and commit as a design decision with costs and evidence. The bounded reader retains at most the configured number of characters in its line string. It reads one additional non-newline character to detect an overlong record but does not append it. The input is not drained after rejection. This gives a concrete retained-line bound without promising a precise process-memory ceiling: string capacity, stream buffers, candidate tasks, index nodes, and rendering copies still consume storage. Each line is split into four short-lived views. Numeric conversion checks both conversion status and complete consumption. Title validation applies the declared ASCII policy. The successful alternative contains an owning Task; no view into the mutable line buffer escapes. A uniqueness set rejects duplicates before the task enters the accepted collection. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: D.4 Keep command-line policy outside the domain
keyPoints: The adapter recognizes --grouped, --help, and at most one input file.
With no file, it borrows standard input.
With a file, a local stream owns the open association and remains alive through loading.
The raw pointer selects one existing stream; it never owns or deletes either target.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 25, treat D.4 Keep command-line policy outside the domain as a design decision with costs and evidence. The adapter recognizes --grouped, --help, and at most one input file. With no file, it borrows standard input. With a file, a local stream owns the open association and remains alive through loading. The raw pointer selects one existing stream; it never owns or deletes either target. The adapter reports structured validation errors with a line number and stable message. It checks final output and flushing before returning normal success. The broad final exception handler is an application boundary for unexpected standard exceptions, not a parser branch that disguises resource failure as malformed data. The core can therefore be tested independently with in-memory streams. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 25, treat D.5 Test the boundary, not just the happy path as a design decision with costs and evidence. The command-line fixture file contains thirty-six cases spanning valid input, empty input, ties, CRLF, final-line policy, title limits, syntax failures, numeric domains, duplicates, file selection, and option handling. The in-process regression below tests a different property: repeated operations on one existing report. It compares accepted state before and after failures instead of starting every experiment from an empty object. BrokenInput throws at a selected byte position. The regression iterates through every failure position in a small two-record candidate, with both ordinary stream-state handling and badbit exceptions enabled. LimitedOutput accepts only eight bytes. The test confirms the error, retained prefix, and unchanged report separately. These fakes control external failure without requiring a full disk, a damaged file, or a network outage. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: D.6 Acceptance review and remaining work
keyPoints: The accepted-state guarantee is supported by a visible commit point and regression checks.
The retained-line bound is supported by checking before append and exact-boundary tests.
Input-consumption behavior is exposed by the failing stream buffer.
Output non-atomicity is exposed by the prefix-retaining sink.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 25, treat D.6 Acceptance review and remaining work as a design decision with costs and evidence. The accepted-state guarantee is supported by a visible commit point and regression checks. The retained-line bound is supported by checking before append and exact-boundary tests. Input-consumption behavior is exposed by the failing stream buffer. Output non-atomicity is exposed by the prefix-retaining sink. These are separate pieces of evidence rather than a single vague claim that the program is “safe.” The extension deliberately omits persistent configuration, authentication, Unicode text policy, crash-durable file publication, asynchronous processing, and concurrent access to a shared report. It also does not impose a total process-memory budget. Those omissions are not hidden behind the successful test count. Adding any of them requires a new contract and representative platform tests. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: This listing is a concrete witness for Appendix D — A Bounded, Transactional Reporting Application. Complete source — main.cpp is not here just to compile; it is here to demonstrate a modern C++ rule. This is build evidence, not runtime behavior. stdout should be empty because no executable path completed. stderr carries the diagnostic: cpp_series/book_02/listings/L0106.cpp:1:10: fatal error: report.hpp: No such file or directory 1 | #include "report.hpp" | ^~~~~~~~~~~~ compilation terminated. The build status is nonzero; do not describe that as the program returning 1. After running or inspecting it, ask which abstraction is doing useful work and which evidence would change if the abstraction were misused.
